title: Secretive SNP condemned over lack of 'transparency as £5bn black hole looms
excerpt: John Swinney's secretive SNP Government refused to set out how it was going to fill a huge £5bn shortfall in the upcoming years as years of financial mismanagement comes back to haunt the Nats.
content:
Secretive John Swinney condemned by own MSPs over lack of 'transparency as £5bn black hole looms

John Swinney's secretive SNP Government refused to set out how it was going to fill a huge £5bn shortfall in the upcoming years as years of financial mismanagement comes back to haunt the Nats.

00:01, 03 Nov 2026

The secretive SNP Government were condemned by a powerful Holyrood committee, headed by a Nat, over a lack of transparency about whether it might plunge into the red by the end of the decade. The Scottish Executive needs to fill a £5bn Budget blackhole by 2030, but its plans to do so are so unclear it has led to a stark warning by the Finance Committee.

‌

‌

MSPs on the committee, headed by SNP backbencher Clare Haughey, demanded that John Swinney provides "much greater transparency" on how it would close its financial void. A "damning" report warned that the budget faces "substantial risks" if the government fails to deliver public service reform, economic growth and taxes.

‌

It was published just a month before Finance Secretary Jenny Gilruth will announce her tax-and-spending plans for the next financial year. The SNP will have to do a deal with at least one other political party in order to get these proposals through Holyrood due to being a minority administration.

‌

Years of economic stagnation, high taxes and expensive freebies has left the public finances in a perilous situation, with Mr Swinney failing to set out a road map to fix this. Instead, he wants to shrink the number of NHS boards and regional councils but has not published any details about what this will look like.

While he tinkers about, Scotland faces “significant financial pressures” with an anticipated fiscal gap of £2.624 billion in resource and £2.146 billion in capital by 2029-30. The country is facing economic pressures from inflation and rising energy prices which are squeezing household incomes and piling pressure on the budget.

The Finance committee declared that it has "insufficient evidence to determine whether the Scottish Government’s tax and spending plans are affordable and sustainable." It went on: "We are also concerned that the Scottish Budget faces substantial risks if the three pillars of the Fiscal Sustainability Delivery Plan (FSDP), including ambitious public service reform targets, are not delivered in full and on time.

‌

"We therefore call on the Scottish Government to provide much greater transparency on progress in closing the fiscal gap and meeting reform targets. As a first step, the Scottish Government should publish an updated FSDP alongside the Scottish Budget 2027-28 on 3 December 2026.

‌

"From 2027, we expect it to resume annual publication of the Medium Term Fiscal Strategy and commit to regular spending reviews, given the greater predictability of the UK review cycle. We also urge it to update its public sector pay policy and tax strategy at the earliest opportunity."

The report was branded "extremely damning" by Scottish Tory finance spokesman Craig Hoy. He went on: "Even one of their own backbenchers who leads this committee says it is typically shrouded in SNP secrecy, and they are unable to fully analyse Swinney’s plans.

‌

“This reeks of more economic incompetence from the nationalists who are already presiding over a £5billion funding gap in Scotland’s finances. Scots who are sick of paying more but getting less deserve to know exactly what the sleekit SNP are planning. Swinney and finance secretary Jenny Gilruth must urgently respond to this report and be fully upfront ahead of the Budget being delivered.”

‌

Clare Haughey, SNP MSP and convener of the Finance and Public Administration Committee, said: “Our committee recognises the scale of the pressure on the Scottish budget, particularly in 2027-28. However, we have insufficient evidence to determine whether the Scottish Government’s tax and spending plans are affordable and sustainable."

The SNP Government had vowed to publish a medium term financial strategy before the end of the year before the Holyrood Election, but Ms Gilruth quietly scrapped this. The committee said that it was "not satisfied with the Cabinet Secretary’s explanation for not providing the document in 2026."

‌

It added: "We would also appreciate more candour if commitments, such as making a fiscal statement, are not to be met." Other concerns were raised about more long-forgotten SNP promises including plans "to reset its approach" to meeting its workforce reduction targets given recent rises in headcount.

Details of how this would happen were requested, as well as "clarification on the Scottish Government's definition of 'frontline' and 'back office' workers under this policy."

‌

On its tax policies, which are often just hiked up without proper consultation and still leading to reduced tax intake, the SNP Executive were urged to "update its tax strategy to provide a strategic and co-ordinated approach to raising revenues, rather than creating individual taxes in isolation."

The Scottish Government has been approached for comment.
